content: Orbital mechanics describes how objects move under gravitational influence, following principles first formalized in Newton's law of universal gravitation and Kepler's laws of planetary motion. Gravitational force between two objects is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: F = G(mâmâ)/rÂ². This creates curved trajectories as gravity continuously accelerates objects toward massive bodies like stars or planets. Closed orbits form when an object's velocity provides sufficient centripetal force to maintain a stable path around a central body without escaping or falling inward. Kepler's first law states that orbits are elliptical with the central body at one focus. The shape of an elliptical orbit is characterized by its eccentricityâa value between 0 (perfect circle) and 1 (parabola, the boundary between closed and open orbits). Kepler's second law, the law of equal areas, indicates that objects move faster when closer to the central body (periapsis) and slower when farther away (apoapsis). Kepler's third law relates orbital period to semi-major axis length: the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis (PÂ² â aÂ³). Orbital energy consists of kinetic energy (from motion) and potential energy (from position in a gravitational field). The sum remains constant in an undisturbed orbit, though energy can transfer between these forms as objects move between periapsis and apoapsis. Changing orbits requires energy expenditure through propulsion systems that provide delta-v (change in velocity). Maneuvers include Hohmann transfers (efficient orbit changes using two engine burns), inclination changes (altering orbital plane orientation), and gravitational assists (using planets' gravity to modify spacecraft trajectories).

scenario.title: Celestial Carousel
scenario.content: Students explore orbital dynamics through an interactive playground simulation where merry-go-rounds represent gravitational systems. The simulation draws parallels between playground physics and celestial mechanics: the spinning platform creates centripetal force analogous to gravity, while objects placed at different distances demonstrate orbital relationships. Students can adjust mass, distance, velocity, and friction to observe how these factors affect orbital stability. The system provides both playground and space visualizations side-by-side, helping students connect familiar experiences with abstract astronomical concepts. Interactive tools allow students to design orbital systems, predict trajectories, and calculate parameters like orbital period, energy, and angular momentum. Challenge scenarios require students to plan orbital transfers, design stable satellite constellations, or navigate complex gravitational environments, teaching fundamental principles of orbital mechanics through intuitive, physically meaningful interactions.

hypothesis.description: Students will analyze orbital dynamics by examining the relationship between gravitational forces and object trajectories. They will predict how mass, distance, and velocity affect orbital characteristics, and calculate parameters like period, energy, and stability for various orbital configurations.
